title: Cosmic Rundown: AI Fatigue, Last.fm Independence, DuckDuckGo Surge
summary: A viral post about AI exhaustion, Last.fm going independent, DuckDuckGo traffic spiking after Google's AI push, and a GitHub outage that disrupted developer workflows.
body_text: The AI Fatigue Conversation A post titled "I'm Tired of Talking to AI" hit the top of Hacker News with over 1,500 points and sparked a massive discussion . The sentiment resonates with a growing segment of users who find AI-generated responses ubiquitous to the point of exhaustion. This comes alongside a TechCrunch piece suggesting "Tech CEOs are apparently suffering from AI psychosis" , which generated its own debate about executive decision-making in the AI gold rush. For teams building AI-powered products, the takeaway is clear: users want AI that genuinely helps, not AI that simply exists to check a box. Thoughtful implementation beats aggressive integration. Last.fm Breaks Free In unexpected news, Last.fm announced its independence . The music tracking service, which has changed hands multiple times over the years, is now operating as a standalone entity. The Hacker News thread features plenty of nostalgia from long-time users and speculation about what this means for the platform's future. For those who remember the CBS Interactive acquisition and the Paramount years, this feels like a return to roots. Whether independence translates to renewed feature development remains to be seen. DuckDuckGo's AI-Free Bump Here's a data point worth noting: DuckDuckGo saw 28% more visits in the week following Google's announcement that users love AI mode. The irony writes itself. The discussion suggests users are actively seeking alternatives when they feel AI is being pushed rather than offered. This aligns with the broader fatigue sentiment and presents an interesting case study in product positioning. GitHub Outage Hits Developer Workflows A significant GitHub incident affected pull requests, issues, git operations, and API requests. The community response ranged from frustration to dark humor about CI/CD pipelines grinding to a halt. These outages serve as reminders about the centralization of developer infrastructure. Teams relying heavily on GitHub Actions for deployment workflows felt the impact most acutely. PostHog's Data Training Decision PostHog announced they will train AI models with user data, opted-in by default . The Hacker News discussion is predictably mixed, with debates about opt-in versus opt-out defaults and what users should reasonably expect from analytics platforms. The broader pattern here matters: as more SaaS tools explore AI features, data usage policies become increasingly important to evaluate. Quick Hits Mini Micro Fantasy Computer : A retro computing project that caught developer attention for its approachable design. See the discussion . Cloudflare Flagship : Cloudflare's new developer platform features generated significant interest with over 300 points and active discussion . Claude Code Workflow Guide : A comprehensive post on using Claude Code as a daily driver covers Claude.md files, skills, subagents, and MCPs. The thread has practical tips from heavy users. What This Means for Content Teams The AI fatigue narrative is not about rejecting AI entirely. It's about demanding better implementation. Users want tools that solve real problems without constant reminders that AI is involved. For content management specifically, this reinforces the value of AI that operates in the background: automating tedious tasks, suggesting improvements, and handling repetitive work without making every interaction feel like a chatbot conversation. The platforms that get this balance right will maintain user trust. The ones that over-index on AI visibility risk the same backlash we're seeing in search and support experiences.

title: Travelers Umbrella Insurance — The Red Umbrella Policy Explained
summary: Learn what Travelers umbrella insurance covers, typical costs for $1M+ coverage, bundling requirements, and how the red umbrella policy compares to standalone carriers like RLI and Markel.
body_text: Travelers Umbrella Insurance — The Red Umbrella Policy Explained If you've ever searched "red umbrella insurance," you're not alone. Thousands of people each month type those words into Google, often without realizing that "red umbrella" refers to a company, not a coverage type. Travelers Insurance, one of the largest property and casualty insurers in the United States, has used its distinctive red umbrella logo for more than a century. The brand recognition is so strong that many consumers now conflate the image with umbrella insurance itself. This article explains what Travelers umbrella insurance actually covers, how much it costs, whether you need to bundle it with other policies, and how it stacks up against standalone umbrella specialists. What Is "Red Umbrella Insurance"? The red umbrella belongs to Travelers Insurance. It does not describe a specific type of coverage. Travelers first adopted the umbrella symbol in 1870, and the company reacquired worldwide trademark rights to the red umbrella logo from Citigroup in 2007 (Travelers, "Travelers Re-acquired Citigroup's Worldwide Rights to the Red Umbrella", 2008) . Today, the logo appears on everything from NASCAR vehicles to stadium advertisements, reinforcing the association between "umbrella" and the Travelers brand. Travelers ranks among the top 10 property and casualty insurers in the U.S. by direct written premium (NAIC, "Market Share Reports", 2026) . The company reported $47.2 billion in net written premium for 2025, with record net income of $5.9 billion (Travelers, "Travelers Reports Excellent Fourth Quarter and Full Year Results", 2026) . Fitch Ratings affirmed Travelers' "AA" Insurer Financial Strength rating with a stable outlook in October 2025 (Fitch Ratings, "Fitch Affirms Travelers Ratings; Outlook Stable", 2025) . The bottom line: "red umbrella insurance" means Travelers. Umbrella insurance itself is a liability coverage category that many carriers offer, from State Farm to specialty providers like RLI and Markel. If you're looking for umbrella coverage, you have options beyond the red umbrella. What Does Travelers Personal Umbrella Insurance Cover? Travelers offers personal umbrella policies that extend liability protection beyond the limits of your underlying homeowners insurance and auto insurance (Travelers, "Umbrella Insurance", 2026) . The policy kicks in when a covered claim exceeds your base policy limits. Coverage Included A Travelers personal umbrella policy typically covers: Bodily injury liability above your auto or home policy limits, such as a serious car accident where medical bills exceed your $300,000 auto limit Property damage liability when you cause damage to someone else's property that exceeds underlying coverage Personal injury claims including defamation, libel, slander, and invasion of privacy Legal defense costs for covered claims, often provided in addition to policy limits Worldwide coverage for incidents that occur outside the United States Claims not covered by underlying policies in certain situations, such as some types of personal liability that fall outside standard home or auto language The Texas Department of Insurance notes that umbrella policies can provide "broader coverage for certain claims that may be excluded by standard policies" (Texas DOI, "Umbrella Policies", 2026) . For example, some umbrella policies cover landlord liability for rental properties not insured under your primary homeowners policy. Available Limits Travelers offers personal umbrella coverage with limits starting at $1 million and extending up to $10 million or higher for qualifying customers (Travelers, "Umbrella Insurance", 2026) . Each additional million typically costs less than the first because the odds of a claim reaching that level decrease with each layer. What Travelers Umbrella Does Not Cover Like all umbrella policies, Travelers excludes certain types of claims: Intentional acts or criminal behavior Business or professional liability (covered by separate commercial policies) Workers' compensation claims Damage to your own property Contractual liability assumed by agreement Claims related to aircraft, watercraft over certain horsepower limits, or recreational vehicles not disclosed on the policy Travelers also requires you to disclose all vehicles, properties, and drivers in your household. Failure to disclose a teenage driver or a rental property could void coverage for related claims. Coverage Type Included in Travelers Umbrella Notes Bodily injury liability Yes Above underlying limits Property damage liability Yes Above underlying limits Personal injury (defamation, libel) Yes Broader than most auto/home policies Legal defense costs Yes Often in addition to limits Intentional acts No Excluded across all carriers Business/professional liability No Requires separate commercial policy Uninsured/underinsured motorist Optional Available as endorsement in some states How Much Does Travelers Umbrella Insurance Cost? Umbrella insurance remains one of the most affordable ways to increase liability protection. According to industry data, the average cost for $1 million in umbrella coverage runs between $150 and $300 per year for most households (Progressive, "Umbrella Insurance Cost", 2026) . Travelers falls within this range for standard-risk customers who bundle home and auto. Factors That Affect Your Premium Travelers prices umbrella policies based on: Number of vehicles and drivers in the household Number of properties you own (primary residence, vacation homes, rental units) Underlying policy limits — higher base limits can mean lower umbrella premiums Claims history and driving records of all household members Net worth and assets — higher-net-worth individuals may need larger limits Location — state insurance regulations and local lawsuit trends affect pricing Youthful drivers — households with drivers under 25 typically pay more Required Underlying Limits Travelers requires minimum liability limits on your underlying home and auto policies before you can purchase umbrella coverage. Typical requirements include: Auto liability: $250,000 per person / $500,000 per accident bodily injury, and $100,000 property damage (250/500/100) Homeowners liability: $300,000 or higher Boat, motorcycle, or RV: Similar elevated limits if applicable These requirements ensure a gap doesn't exist between where your underlying policy ends and your umbrella begins. If you currently carry lower limits (like 100/300/50 auto liability), you'll need to increase them before Travelers will write an umbrella policy. Bundling Discounts Travelers offers multi-policy discounts when you combine home, auto, and umbrella coverage (Travelers, "Bundle Your Policies", 2026) . The discount varies by state but typically ranges from 5% to 15% off combined premiums. Bundling also simplifies claims coordination, since one carrier handles all related liability coverage. Do You Have to Bundle Umbrella with Travelers Home or Auto? Yes. Travelers typically requires you to hold a homeowners or auto policy with them before they'll issue a personal umbrella (Travelers, "Umbrella Insurance", 2026) . This bundling requirement reflects how most large personal-lines carriers operate. State Farm, Allstate, Liberty Mutual, and USAA all follow similar models. Why Carriers Require Bundling Bundled umbrella policies work because the carrier controls both the underlying and excess layers. When Travelers writes your home, auto, and umbrella, they know: Your exact underlying limits Your claims history across all policies Household composition and risk profile That no coverage gaps exist between layers This integration means smoother claims handling. If someone sues you after a car accident and the claim exceeds your $500,000 auto limit, Travelers can coordinate between their auto claims team and their umbrella team without waiting for information from a third party. Drawbacks of the Bundled Model Bundling creates trade-offs: Less flexibility — if Travelers raises your home or auto rates, you can't easily shop around without losing your umbrella Carrier exit risk — if Travelers decides to pull out of your state (as some carriers have done in California and Florida), you lose all three policies Potentially higher combined cost — another carrier might offer better home rates, but you'd need to find a separate umbrella solution The Coverage Cat guide on buying umbrella separately from auto or home insurance explains when this flexibility matters most, such as when you live in a state with limited carrier availability or have non-standard insurance needs. Travelers Availability by State Travelers writes personal umbrella insurance in most U.S. states, but availability and pricing vary. The company has been more selective in catastrophe-prone markets, though it continues to offer policies in states like Florida, Texas, and California where some competitors have retreated. Check with a Travelers agent or broker to confirm current availability in your area. Travelers Umbrella vs. Standalone Umbrella Carriers Not everyone wants to bundle. If your home insurer dropped you due to wildfire risk, or if you simply found better rates elsewhere, you might need a standalone umbrella policy . Standalone carriers don't require you to hold underlying policies with them. Major Standalone Options Three carriers dominate the standalone umbrella market: RLI Insurance offers personal umbrella coverage in all 50 states through independent agents. RLI allows underlying policies from any carrier and offers limits from $1 million to $5 million (RLI, "Personal Umbrella Insurance", 2026) . Markel provides personal umbrella through select brokers, with a reputation for accepting higher-risk profiles and offering competitive pricing for customers with multiple properties or vehicles. Monoline (USLI) specializes exclusively in umbrella coverage and accepts underlying policies from any admitted carrier (Monoline, "Top Standalone Personal Umbrella Insurance Carriers", 2026) . USLI (United States Liability Insurance Group) underwrites Monoline policies. For a detailed breakdown, see the Coverage Cat comparison of standalone umbrella carriers . Financial Strength Comparison All major umbrella carriers maintain strong financial ratings, which matters because umbrella claims can reach millions of dollars. Carrier AM Best Rating Fitch Rating Model Travelers A++ (Superior) AA Bundled RLI A+ (Superior) Not rated Standalone Markel A (Excellent) A+ Standalone USLI (Monoline) A++ (Superior) Not rated Standalone Chubb A++ (Superior) AA Both Travelers holds the highest possible AM Best rating (A++ Superior), as does USLI. RLI carries an A+ rating, still considered "Superior" by AM Best standards. All of these carriers have decades of claims-paying history. Coverage Differences Most umbrella policies cover similar core exposures, but some differences exist: Personal injury breadth — some standalone policies offer broader definitions of personal injury, covering more types of defamation or privacy claims Uninsured/underinsured motorist — availability varies by carrier and state Underlying limit requirements — standalone carriers sometimes accept lower underlying limits than bundled carriers Watercraft and recreational vehicle coverage — limits on horsepower and engine size vary Chubb's personal umbrella, for example, includes coverage for executive liability and employment practices for domestic workers (Chubb, "Personal Umbrella Excess Liability", 2026) . These enhanced features target high-net-worth households with staff, rental properties, and multiple residences. When to Choose Travelers vs. Standalone Consider Travelers umbrella if: You already hold home and auto with Travelers and are satisfied with pricing You prefer single-carrier simplicity for claims coordination You qualify for bundling discounts that make the combined premium competitive Travelers maintains strong availability in your state Consider standalone umbrella if: Your home insurer doesn't offer umbrella or requires limits you don't want You've been non-renewed or dropped by a carrier in a high-risk market You want to shop home and auto independently without losing umbrella coverage You have non-standard exposures (high-value assets, multiple rental properties, unique vehicles) that a specialty carrier handles better The right choice depends on your specific situation. Many households in stable markets find bundling convenient and cost-effective. Those in volatile insurance markets, like parts of California, Florida, or Louisiana, often benefit from the flexibility that standalone policies provide. Getting Umbrella Coverage Whether you choose Travelers or a standalone option, umbrella insurance remains one of the most efficient ways to protect your assets. A million-dollar lawsuit can wipe out years of savings in months. Umbrella coverage provides a buffer, typically for less than a dollar a day. To compare quotes, you can work with an independent insurance agent who represents multiple carriers, or use an online platform that shows options side by side. Travelers policies are available through their captive agents and select independent brokers. Standalone options like RLI and Monoline are typically sold through independent agents. For more information on umbrella coverage, see the Coverage Cat umbrella insurance guide , which explains who needs umbrella, how limits work, and how to determine the right amount for your situation.

title: Introducing Basedash Skills
summary: Skills are reusable bundles of instructions that every Basedash AI surface — chat, charts, dashboards, automations, insights, and tasks — can read on demand.…
body_text: Today we’re launching Skills — reusable bundles of instructions that every Basedash AI surface can read on demand. You define a concept once — how your team calculates activation, which fields matter for support triage, what makes a clean revenue breakdown — and every agent in Basedash picks it up automatically. No more pasting the same caveats into every prompt. No more drift between teams about what a metric actually means. Teach Basedash once. It learns everywhere. Why we built it AI is great at producing answers and terrible at remembering rules. Anyone who has used a chat-based BI tool for more than a few days has run into the same problem: you can describe what activation means once, but the next person asking the same question gets a different definition. The system has no memory of how your team thinks about its data. We’ve watched our own team work around this for the past few weeks. Whenever someone asked the chat agent about “MRR” or “activation rate”, they’d quietly include the same definition in their prompt — “trials excluded, GAAP only, calendar weeks in UTC”. The definition was implicitly the team’s, but the AI had no way to know that. Skills are how we move those definitions out of one-off prompts and into shared, durable context. They sit somewhere between a system prompt and a semantic layer: more structured than free-form context, lighter than dbt models. How Skills work A skill is a name and a few lines of plain-language instructions. There’s no schema to follow, no SQL to write — you describe the concept the way you’d brief a new analyst. Write a skill. An admin opens Settings → AI context and creates a skill with a name and a few lines of instructions — how a metric is defined, when to use a specific chart type, or which fields matter. AI reads it on demand. Every agent in Basedash gets a lightweight catalogue of skill names in its system prompt. When a skill looks relevant to the current request, the agent loads its full instructions through a tool call you can see right in the thinking trace. Every surface uses it. The same catalogue feeds chat, the chart builder, dashboards, automations, insights, and background tasks. One definition, every agent. Crucially, there’s no semantic search or black-box retrieval here. The agent decides which skill is relevant based on the name + the context of the request, and you can see exactly which skills it loaded for any given answer. Auditable by design. What a good skill looks like Skills work best when each one focuses on a single concept or workflow. A few patterns we’ve seen work well internally: Activation rate. “Activation = signed up and completed onboarding within 7 days. Exclude trial-only accounts and internal email domains. Use calendar weeks in UTC; weeks start on Monday. Always compare cohorts by signup_month.” Revenue analysis. “MRR is GAAP recurring revenue, excluding trial accounts. Always segment revenue by plan tier in any breakdown. When comparing periods, use calendar months in UTC.” Support triage. “Group tickets by category and priority before summarizing. Tickets open longer than 48 hours are SLA risk. Use human-readable status names, not raw enum values.” Experiments. “A/B reports use exposure_first events, 7-day windows, and always include p-values. Treatment and control are denoted by the variant column.” A skill can be anywhere from a single line to a few paragraphs — up to 50,000 characters, so even your most nuanced playbooks fit. Skills are the natural home for the kinds of conventions that used to live in a Notion page nobody reads. Skills as a lightweight semantic layer The use case we get most excited about: skills as a lightweight semantic layer for metrics. Every B2B SaaS company has its own definition of MRR, activation, churn, and retention — and “lightweight” is the operative word here. You don’t have to model your entire warehouse in dbt to start codifying the metrics that matter. You write a skill called “Activation rate” once. It explains how to calculate it, which accounts to exclude, what time window to use, and what chart you prefer. From then on, anyone in your organization who asks the AI about activation gets a consistent answer — whether they’re chatting with the agent, building a dashboard, or scheduling a weekly report. The chart builder lays it out the way you specified. The automation runs use the same rules. The insights agent surfaces trends in the right units. This is the part where the multi-surface story matters. A semantic layer that only powers one feature is just an opinionated function. A semantic layer that powers every AI surface in your BI tool is something else: a shared brain that gets smarter every time someone adds a skill. How we use Skills at Basedash We’ve been running on Skills internally for the past several weeks, and they’ve quietly become some of the most reached-for context in our workspace. Our growth team wrote an “Activation rate” skill on day one — the definition was already on a Notion page, so it took five minutes to port over. Now nobody has to remember the trial exclusion rule when asking the agent about weekly activation. Our finance team’s “Revenue analysis” skill is the reason every chart in our exec dashboards uses GAAP and excludes trials, even when the person building it didn’t know to specify. Our support team’s triage skill means automation-generated weekly summaries categorize tickets the way humans would. The compounding effect is real. We started with three skills, and now we’re at fifteen. Each new one removes another thing the team had to remember to type into a prompt — and every existing dashboard and automation gets a little smarter without anyone touching them. Getting started Skills are available today for all Basedash users. Sign up for Basedash (or log in) As an admin, go to Settings → Organization → AI context Click New skill and write your first one — try a metric you’ve explained more than once Ask the chat agent about it and watch the Reading {name} skill step appear in the trace For setup tips and best practices, see the Skills feature page or the AI context docs . What’s next Skills round out our story for shared, durable AI context. Combined with global context for org-wide facts, Insights for proactive findings, Dashboards for AI-built reports, and Automations for scheduled work, Basedash now has a place for every layer of how teams encode their business in AI. We’re going to keep investing here — letting anyone in your org propose a skill, surfacing which skills were loaded for any given answer, and helping agents author new skills as they learn what your team cares about. The shape we’re chasing: a BI tool that gets sharper the longer you use it. Write your first skill today and stop re-explaining what your metrics mean.

body_text: London, United Kingdom, 13 May 2026 – SOPHiA GENETICS (NASDAQ: SOPH), a global leader in Ai-driven precision medicine, today announced a collaboration with Synnovis, one of England’s leading pathology providers, to bring liquid biopsy testing to lung and breast cancer patients across the U.K. as part of NHS England’s ‘ revolutionary blood test-first ’ program. Synnovis, a major provider for England’s South East Genomic Medicine Service, worked with SOPHiA GENETICS to launch the liquid biopsy test MSK-ACCESS® powered with SOPHiA DDMTM. This innovative test, originally developed by Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, detects actionable genomic alterations from a single blood draw and leverages state-of-the-art Ai to analyze circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in a minimally invasive manner. The new blood-based test offered by Synnovis can help fast-track cancer patients to receive targeted therapy up to two weeks earlier, while helping some avoid further tests and invasive treatments such as chemotherapy. Following the successful pilot program, Synnovis is already supporting approximately 400 patients per month with ctDNA liquid biopsy testing and is demonstrating the real-world impact of this advanced care. In one case, a patient with suspected advanced lung cancer was able to receive a ctDNA-informed personalised treatment plan within just two weeks. In another case, providers used SOPHiA DDMTM to identify new genetic variants for a patient who had been living with breast cancer for more than 15 years, unlocking additional treatment options and potential eligibility for clinical trials. Synnovis and SOPHiA GENETICS anticipate that the application will be used to test approximately 7,000 breast and lung cancer patients annually, or roughly one third of all ctDNA tests in England, as the demand for liquid biopsy testing increases. Persephone du Parcq, MSc., Lead Translational Scientist, Synnovis, said : “Liquid biopsy testing simplifies how we generate genomic insights. A routine blood draw can reveal information from multiple tumour sites and speed up delivery of results to the patients. It also broadens access for patients who cannot tolerate invasive procedures or travel to specialist hospitals. As adoption increases, this approach will substantially expand the reach and impact of genomic testing services, and we anticipate economic savings for healthcare providers and better outcomes for greater numbers of patients.” Ross Muken, President, SOPHiA GENETICS, said : “Synnovis plays a vital role in delivering genomic testing services to patients across South East England, and this collaboration reflects what becomes possible when world-class pathology infrastructure meets scalable Ai-driven analysis. With roughly one third of all ctDNA testing in England expected to run through this programme, we see this as a defining moment for liquid biopsy at scale within the NHS , and a model for how health systems in Europe can make precision oncology accessible. Beyond accelerating targeted treatments, MSK-ACCESS® powered with SOPHiA DDMTM provides Synnovis with the flexibility to incorporate additional indications as they are introduced into future NHS cancer screening programs. It also utilizes a matched tumor-normal approach as well as technology from AccuGenomics® to improve accuracy and avoid false positives. Leading laboratories like Synnovis are helping bring NHS England’s ‘blood test-first’ approach to scale through innovative solutions, contributing to a sustainable, data-driven approach to cancer care across the United Kingdom. By strengthening its genomic testing infrastructure, Synnovis joins a growing network of NHS institutions using SOPHiA GENETICS’ technology to conduct local analysis, maintain alignment with NHS data-security standards, and support the operational model of distributed analysis hubs. To learn more about how Synnovis deployed ctDNA testing for the patients it serves, view a webinar presented by one of the laboratory’s lead scientists.
